content.cons:
Responding to Steve Hughes’ BS recent post on LinkedIn….

I eventually made it to uni, even though my career took a different path.
So I have to admit, it was exciting finding myself at the University of Cambridge recently, back in the classroom at Judge Business School with many of our senior leaders. It felt inspiring, motivating and a 'pinch myself' moment with a little bit of what might have been...
I was there for our Leading with Al programme, delivered by Cambridge Spark, exploring one of the biggest opportunities, and challenges, facing society and our industry. I was keen to explore whether this would be a catalyst for another industrial revolution.
I went in with one message for everyone taking part: be curious, because there's a huge amount to learn.
Al has the ability help us spot fraud, remove pain points for customers, make better decisions and free colleagues up to focus on the things humans do best. I have no doubt that upskilling our leaders means realising greater future potential for the Group.
But in financial services, the human bit really matters - real people complementing the power of Al.

We studied the case of radiology, a profession where Al has the power to read scans better than humans. But while Al can do that one task better than a human, it can't do any of the other 26 tasks a radiologist completes with a patient.

In our world, a system might spot an unusual transaction. A colleague can spot that someone doesn't seem themselves. They can hear something in a customer's voice, understand vulnerability or simply listen when someone needs to talk.

That's why, for us at Coventry Building Society, we talk about digital first, human always.

Really??? Human always….. which is why you’ve just made a circa 500 people redundant before Christmas 2026!! 

Very human / humane in deed. 

Well done!

content.cons:
The current approach to transformation feels short-sighted. Experienced staff have been made redundant in favour of an AI tool that, in my view, hasn’t yet demonstrated that it can fully replace the knowledge and experience being lost. I’m not against AI or progress, but removing skilled people before the technology and processes are properly established seems a huge risk.

This is especially concerning for a financial institution, where testing, audit requirements and reliable systems are essential. There are longstanding issues with legacy technology and testing environments that still need addressing. Investing in new tools while leaving these underlying problems unresolved feels like the wrong priority.

The impact on remaining colleagues is also concerning. People are taking on more responsibility, workloads are increasing, and there is uncertainty about new roles and how teams are expected to work. The integration with the Co-operative Bank appears to be adding to these problems, with conflicting approaches to delivery and little evidence of a joined-up way forward.

There are also serious questions about leadership and decision-making. Confidence in management is being undermined by a perception that progression doesn’t always reflect ability, alongside a lack of clear direction and accountability. At a time when colleagues need reassurance and support, too many seem to be left with uncertainty instead.

Finally, responding to critical Glassdoor reviews with the same comment that “change is difficult” misses the point. People aren’t necessarily opposed to change; they’re concerned about how it’s being handled. Dismissing those concerns rather than properly addressing them only reinforces the feeling that colleagues aren’t being listened to.
content.pros: The Coventry used to feel like an organisation that genuinely cared about it’s customers, it’s colleagues and it’s communities. Doing the right thing seemed to matter. It’s disappointing to see that culture appear to be increasingly replaced by a focus only on the bottom line.
content.advice:
Take a step back and consider the longer-term consequences of these decisions. Make sure new technology is genuinely ready before removing the people and expertise it is supposed to replace. Address the underlying technical issues, get Coventry and Co-op working towards a shared plan, and give colleagues clear direction and support.

I’m raising these concerns because I believe the Coventry risks losing more than experienced staff. It risks losing the knowledge, culture and customer-focused values that made it a good organisation to work for in the first place.

Change isn’t the problem. It’s the way that change is being managed, and the apparent lack of consideration for the consequences, that should concern people.
content.summary: Caring culture replaced by focus on profit alone

content.cons:
I'd worked for the Co-operative Bank for 14 years before the takeover by Coventry Building Society. Having dedicated such a significant part of my career to the organisation, I was understandably saddened by the deterioration in the working environment following the takeover from CBS.

From the outset, there appeared to be a clear divide between the existing Co-operative Bank employees and those from Coventry Building Society. Rather than fostering an inclusive culture built on mutual respect, collaboration and shared objectives, the environment became increasingly divisive and, at times, deeply hostile.

A source of frustration was the way collaborative working was initially presented. Workstreams were introduced as opportunities for genuine collaboration between the existing Co-operative Bank teams and Coventry Building Society colleagues. However, in practice, we would invest considerable time and effort into these collaborative exercises, only for Coventry colleagues to subsequently pursue their own approach, disregard the work we had produced, or dismiss our contributions altogether. This made the entire process feel disingenuous and resulted in significant time and effort being wasted on work that appeared never to have been genuinely considered. If the intention was always for Coventry Building Society to impose its own processes and decisions, a transparent and honest approach from the outset would have been far more respectful and efficient. Instead, the repeated presentation of these exercises as collaborative, when my experience suggested that our input was not being meaningfully valued, undermined trust and left colleagues feeling that their expertise, time and contributions were being treated with little regard.

My experience was of a team culture in which certain individuals appeared willing to misrepresent situations, make inaccurate claims and undermine colleagues' contributions in order to protect their own reputations or present themselves in a more favourable light. Work that colleagues had invested considerable time and effort into producing could seemingly be disregarded or treated as though it had never existed. When concerns were challenged, there was little evidence of meaningful investigation, accountability or acknowledgement of wrongdoing. Apologies were conspicuously absent, and there appeared to be an assumption that the Coventry Building Society approach was automatically the correct one, regardless of the circumstances or the perspectives of others.

The behaviour I witnessed went beyond ordinary workplace disagreements. It created an atmosphere in which unprofessional conduct, personal hostility and what I perceived to be bullying tactics were allowed to persist. In my experience, the leadership responsible for overseeing this team failed to address these issues adequately, leaving colleagues to work in an environment where they did not feel consistently respected or treated fairly.

The shortcomings in leadership extended beyond the immediate team. During periods of significant uncertainty, including organisational restructuring, the area leader would reassure colleagues during town hall calls that support was available and that anyone who needed help was welcome to approach him. Unfortunately, my experience did not reflect those assurances. When encountering him in person, I found that attempts to engage could be met with apparent avoidance, while there also seemed to be a reluctance to acknowledge or address the difficulties colleagues were experiencing. This created a significant disconnect between the supportive leadership message communicated publicly and the support that appeared to be available in practice.

I also found aspects of the executive leadership culture deeply disappointing. One particularly memorable example involved a colleague who was due to deliver a presentation and had openly acknowledged beforehand that they were extremely nervous. While the colleague was presenting, the executive leading the call asked participants to share what they were watching on television in the Teams chat. Responses began appearing in quick succession, creating an unnecessary distraction. Even after the presenter explicitly stated that the activity was distracting them, it continued. I considered this behaviour wholly inappropriate, particularly given the presenter's evident vulnerability and the importance of demonstrating professionalism, respect and support from senior leaders.

Examples such as this reinforced my concerns about the standards of leadership, the lack of consideration shown to colleagues and the apparent absence of accountability at senior levels. Leaders set the tone for an organisation, and I believe their conduct should reflect the values of respect, integrity, fairness and professionalism they expect from others.

Having spent 16 years working for the Co-operative Bank, I understand the importance of a positive workplace culture, effective leadership and treating colleagues with dignity. What I experienced following the takeover fell significantly short of those expectations. I found the environment hostile, divisive and unnecessarily unpleasant, with insufficient evidence that concerns about behaviour were being addressed effectively.

Although I was extremely sad to be made redundant from the Co-operative Bank after so many years of service, the experience fundamentally changed my perception of Coventry Building Society as an employer. I would not choose to work for the organisation, as the culture I experienced was incompatible with my own professional values and expectations of ethical leadership.

Ultimately, the most disappointing aspect was not simply the change in employer, but the apparent failure to establish a workplace culture in which people felt respected, supported and confident that they would be treated fairly. After 16 years of service to the Co-operative Bank, I believe employees deserved considerably better.
content.pros:
The two positives I can identify are the cleanliness of the toilets at the Binley site and the introduction of free fruit and access to clean drinking water. These were welcome provisions that I had not experienced to the same standard at the Co-operative Bank's main site, where I had significant concerns about toilet cleanliness and hygiene.

Beyond these basic facilities, I struggle to identify any other positive aspects of my experience of Coventry Building Society following the takeover.
content.advice:
My advice to management would be to undertake a serious and honest review of their leadership capabilities, management practices and the culture they have allowed to develop.

Leadership training should be an immediate priority. In my experience, the standard of leadership was exceptionally poor, with a concerning lack of accountability, professionalism, empathy and respect for employees. The way colleagues were treated was deeply disappointing and, at times, completely unacceptable. Leaders need to understand that their responsibility extends beyond delivering business objectives; they are also responsible for creating an environment in which employees feel valued, supported and able to raise concerns without fear of being undermined or dismissed.

The organisation also needs to reflect seriously on the loss of experienced and knowledgeable employees. By failing to recognise the value of existing staff, their expertise and their contributions, Coventry Building Society risks losing an enormous amount of institutional knowledge. In my view, this has already been a significant issue. The long-term consequences of losing people who understand the business, its processes, its customers and its regulatory obligations should not be underestimated.

I am particularly concerned about the potential implications for risk management and regulatory compliance. During my experience, I felt that attention to detail and the importance of established risk and regulatory processes were not always given the consideration they deserved. In a regulated financial services environment, this is a serious concern. Weak leadership, the loss of experienced employees and the erosion of organisational knowledge can create significant vulnerabilities, potentially increasing the risk of regulatory breaches, financial penalties and, most importantly, customer harm.

Management needs to recognise that a culture in which employees feel disregarded, collaboration is perceived as disingenuous and concerns are not properly addressed is neither sustainable nor conducive to good business outcomes. Reassurances about supporting colleagues mean very little if leadership behaviour does not reflect those commitments in practice.

Ultimately, Coventry Building Society needs to look beyond its own management hierarchy, listen meaningfully to the people doing the work and take responsibility for the consequences of its decisions. The standard of leadership I experienced was embarrassingly poor. Unless there is genuine accountability, meaningful leadership development and a fundamental improvement in how employees are treated, the organisation risks continuing to lose talented people while undermining the very expertise and operational knowledge it needs to succeed.

My strongest advice is this: treat your employees with respect, invest in competent leadership, take risk and regulation seriously, and stop assuming that seniority automatically equates to good judgement.

Another significant concern related to the apparent lack of transparency surrounding organisational restructures. On several occasions, it appeared that members of the Coventry Building Society talent team had advance insight into the proposed structure before it was formally announced to employees. In one particularly notable instance, a colleague indicated that she would be taking on a role that did not yet formally exist. When the restructure was subsequently announced, a role was created that appeared to correspond exactly with what she had previously described. Similar situations occurred on multiple occasions, raising serious questions about how much information was being shared in advance, who had access to it, and whether all employees were being treated fairly and consistently throughout the process.

The perception that certain individuals may have had prior knowledge of proposed roles and organisational decisions, while others were left in uncertainty, was deeply concerning. Restructuring processes should be conducted with transparency, integrity and appropriate confidentiality, with employees having confidence that decisions are being made fairly and in accordance with relevant employment legislation and internal procedures. The apparent discrepancies I observed significantly undermined that confidence and raised questions about the integrity of the process. At the very least, I believe these circumstances warranted greater scrutiny and a clear explanation from management.
content.summary: A deeply disappointing workplace culture, poor leadership, a lack of accountability and unprofessional behaviour

One co-worker gives patients sleeping pills without consent to make work easier. Another retaliates against them for asking to use the restroom or be changed. Some residents believe this caused long-term harm, but it's hard to prove. Many residents appeared sick, likely from foodborne illness after eating, which occurred at least once a week. Residents pay 5,000 pounds a month, but lack towels etc. Residents feel unheard.
